title: Trim a Binary Search Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: rebuilding a new BST from scratch versus in-place recursive trimming that reuses existing nodes.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary search tree and the bounds low and high, trim the tree so that all its values are within [low, high]. Trimming may require changing the root, and the result must still be a valid BST. Return the trimmed tree's root.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root (a BST), low, high"],["Output","The root of the trimmed BST, containing only values in [low,high]"],["Goal","Trim in place, reusing existing nodes, exploiting the BST property to skip entire subtrees"],["Constraints","Up to 10^4 nodes"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"BST\" plus \"keep only values in a range\"","Use BST ordering: if a node is out of range on one side, its entire corresponding subtree can be discarded, and the OTHER side's trimmed result replaces it"],["Result must remain a valid BST","Reattaching a trimmed subtree directly (not rebuilding from scratch) preserves the BST structure automatically"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

If a node's value is below low, that node and its ENTIRE left subtree are too small and can be discarded; the trimmed result of its right subtree should take this node's place. Symmetrically for a node above high. If a node is within range, both its subtrees are recursively trimmed and reattached.

blocks.title: Analogy: Pruning a Family Tree to Only Include a Range of Birth Years
blocks.text: Picture pruning a family tree to keep only people born within a certain year range. If an ancestor is too early, everyone descended in that particular branch through them who is EVEN EARLIER can also be discarded, but their later descendants might still qualify and should be reattached in their place.

blocks.caption: An out-of-range node is replaced by the trimmed result of its relevant single subtree

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: root = [1,0,2], low=1, high=2
Result (preorder): 1 null 2 null null. Node 0 is below low=1 and is removed, replaced by nothing (it had no valid right subtree).
5. How Should We Think?

Before rebuilding a new tree from scratch out of the in-range values, notice that trimming can be done recursively in place: an out-of-range node is simply replaced by the (recursively trimmed) subtree on the side that could still contain valid values.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If root.val < low, the entire left subtree is guaranteed even smaller, so discard it; the answer for this subtree is whatever trimBST returns for the RIGHT subtree.

Observation 2: Symmetrically, if root.val > high, discard the right subtree, using the trimmed LEFT subtree instead.

Observation 3: If root.val is within range, recursively trim both children and reattach them directly to this node.

Observation 4: This reuses existing nodes throughout, requiring no new node creation, and correctly produces a valid BST since BST ordering is preserved by construction.
This leads to a recursive trim: if out of range on one side, recurse into and return the other side's trimmed result; otherwise, trim both children and reattach them to the current node.
6. Brute Force Solution
Collect all in-range values via a traversal, then rebuild a brand new BST from scratch by inserting them one at a time.
Why the code is written this way

items: Rebuilding from scratch directly produces a valid BST containing only in-range values.
It discards the existing tree structure entirely and creates all new nodes, wasting the reusable parts of the original tree.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) worst case if rebuilding via naive insertion.
Space: O(n) for new nodes.
Limitation: in-place recursive trimming reuses existing nodes and structure, avoiding any new node creation.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Instead of discarding the whole tree, recursively trim in place: an out-of-range node is directly replaced by the trimmed result of its one potentially-valid subtree, while in-range nodes simply get their children replaced by their own trimmed versions.
Recursively: if val < low, return trim(right); if val > high, return trim(left); otherwise, set left = trim(left), right = trim(right), return this node.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for root = [1,0,2], low=1, high=2

blocks.content: {"headers":["Node","Action"],"rows":[["1","in range, trim both children"],["0","0<1, discard, return trim(right)=null"],["2","in range, keep"]]}

blocks.text: Why This Works

The BST property guarantees an out-of-range node's corresponding subtree contains only values even further out of range, so discarding it and using the OTHER side's trimmed result directly correctly reattaches any still-valid values, all while reusing existing nodes and preserving BST ordering.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n).
Space: O(height) recursion depth, no new nodes.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Rebuild from scratch","O(n squared) worst case","O(n) new nodes"],["In-place recursive trim","O(n)","O(height) extra","The expected, efficient solution."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Trim a Binary Search Tree demonstrates in-place subtree replacement using the BST property, avoiding any need to rebuild the tree from scratch.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to reattach the trimmed subtree back to the parent (root.left = ..., root.right = ...).
Not returning the correct replacement subtree when the current node itself is out of range.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["The entire tree is outside [low,high]","Returns null."],["The entire tree is already within [low,high]","Returns the tree unchanged."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Stating "an out-of-range node is simply replaced by its relevant trimmed subtree" clarifies the elegant in-place recursive structure.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "trim a BST to a value range", think: an out-of-range node is replaced by the trimmed result of its one relevant subtree.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you also count how many nodes were removed?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Range Sum of BST, using the identical subtree-pruning technique for a different goal.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Rebuilding from scratch costs O(n squared) worst case and O(n) new nodes; in-place recursive trimming costs O(n) time and O(height) extra space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: in-place recursive subtree replacement using BST ordering.
Core Idea: an out-of-range node is replaced by the trimmed result of its relevant single subtree; in-range nodes get both children trimmed and reattached.
Time: O(n squared) for rebuilding, O(n) for in-place trimming.
Space: O(n) new nodes versus O(height) extra.
Most Important Observation: an out-of-range node's irrelevant subtree can be discarded entirely, reusing the relevant one directly.
Interview Difficulty: an accessible, elegant BST manipulation problem.
One line memory trick: out-of-range node is replaced by its relevant trimmed subtree.
